meta.title: Who really said "How Do You Get To Carnegie Hall? Practice!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Arthur Rubinstein. The joke's earliest known tellings, in two 1955 newspaper columns, name no musician at all. Heifetz came later, and only as rumor.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'How Do You Get To Carnegie Hall? Practice!'?
meta.ogDescription: Two 1955 humor columns give the line to an unnamed maestro. Jascha Heifetz was attached later that year, as rumor. Rubinstein is in no early source.

answer.label: Not Arthur Rubinstein — an anonymous 1955 newspaper gag
answer.authorDates: First in print, 1955 · no musician named in any early telling
answer.sourceLine: Arthur Rubinstein is the name most often attached to this line today, but he appears in none of its early citations. The two earliest known tellings — the Philadelphia Tribune of 1 January 1955 and E. E. Kenyon’s syndicated “Wit Parade” column of 13 March 1955 — hand the punchline to an anonymous “absent-minded music professor” and an anonymous “absent-minded maestro.” Jascha Heifetz was the first musician named, later the same year, and even then only as “rumor.” No documented source puts the line in Rubinstein’s mouth.

source.heading: The paper trail runs back to 1955, and stops

docMeta.dd: Jascha Heifetz, in Bennett Cerf’s column, 9 November 1955 — as “rumor”

source.excerpt:
The absent-minded maestro was racing up New York’s Seventh Avenue to a rehearsal, when a stranger stopped him. “Pardon me,” he said, “can you tell me how to get to Carnegie Hall?”
“Yes,” answered the maestro breathlessly. “Practice!”
source.trailTitle: How the joke acquired a face
trail: 1 January 1955 — the first sighting, and nobody famous is in it. Barry Popik’s Big Apple entry ↗ transcribes a Philadelphia Tribune column in which an “absent-minded music professor,” rushing to a late appointment, is stopped in the street and answers: “Practice constantly.”

13 March 1955 — the punchline sharpens to one word. Quote Investigator ↗ names E. E. Kenyon’s “The Wit Parade” in the Washington Post as the joke’s earliest known appearance. The speaker is still only “the absent-minded maestro,” and the word practice is said once.

9 November 1955 — a celebrity name is attached, and hedged. Bennett Cerf’s “Try and Stop Me” column runs it as “Rumor is that a pedestrian in Manhattan stopped Jascha Heifetz…” — transcribed by Popik ↗, and reprinted in Cerf’s 1956 book The Life of the Party.

Arthur Rubinstein arrives late, and from nowhere. Wikipedia’s survey of the joke’s folklore ↗ lists Rubinstein among later substitutes for Heifetz — alongside an unnamed beatnik, a bopper and Dizzy Gillespie — and states plainly that the joke’s origins remain a mystery.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator names this — E. E. Kenyon’s syndicated column “The Wit Parade,” Washington Post, 13 March 1955 — as the joke’s earliest known appearance, and notes that in this version the word practice is not repeated. Barry Popik’s chronology records an earlier one still: the Philadelphia Tribune of 1 January 1955, where an “absent-minded music professor” answers “Practice constantly.” Neither names a musician.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author, so no copyright status can be asserted for it and quotle.info makes no public-domain claim here. The two 1955 newspaper columns carrying the earliest known versions are themselves 1955 publications, and both present the gag as one already in circulation — the Philadelphia Tribune introduces it as “the one about the absent-minded music professor” — rather than as original composition, so neither column establishes authorship of the line.

author.name: Jascha Heifetz
author.kicker: The first name it was pinned to
author.heading: Jascha Heifetz — and even that was only rumor
author.bio: Jascha Heifetz (1901–1987) was a Lithuanian-born American violinist, among the most celebrated instrumentalists of his era. He is not the author of this joke — but he is the first person the joke is known to have been attached to, in Bennett Cerf’s syndicated humor column of 9 November 1955 — the earliest naming in Popik’s chronology — which offered the story as hearsay rather than fact: “Rumor is that a pedestrian in Manhattan stopped Jascha Heifetz…” Cerf reprinted it in his 1956 anthology The Life of the Party, and from there the gag travelled. Arthur Rubinstein was substituted for Heifetz only later, with no source behind the swap.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in print in 1955, with no musician named: Jimmy Brown, “These Foolish Things,” Philadelphia Tribune, January 1, 1955, 12; and E. E. Kenyon, “The Wit Parade,” Washington Post, March 13, 1955, AW22. Both transcribed in Barry Popik, “‘How do you get to Carnegie Hall?’ (joke),” The Big Apple, July 5, 2004. The first named musician is Jascha Heifetz, offered as rumor in Bennett Cerf, “Try and Stop Me,” Titusville Herald, November 9, 1955, 4, and reprinted in Cerf’s The Life of the Party (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1956), 335. The attribution to Arthur Rubinstein is unsupported by any source from the period.

copyAttribution: "How do you get to Carnegie Hall? Practice!" — not Arthur Rubinstein. The joke's earliest known appearances, in two 1955 newspaper humor columns, give the line to an unnamed musician: an "absent-minded music professor" (Philadelphia Tribune, 1 January 1955) and an "absent-minded maestro" (Washington Post, 13 March 1955). The first named musician, Jascha Heifetz, was attached later that same year by Bennett Cerf, and only as "rumor." Rubinstein appears in no source from the period. Origin unknown. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-repeated lines in music, and almost every element of the popular version is a later accretion — the tripled punchline, the street corner, and above all the man supposedly saying it.

items.why: Rubinstein is the name most often attached to the joke today, but he appears in none of the early citations: Popik’s chronology ↗ runs from January 1955 to March 1961 without him. Wikiquote’s Arthur Rubinstein page ↗ does not carry the line in any section at all.

The first named musician — but the source that named him did not vouch for it. Bennett Cerf introduced the story as “Rumor is that…” in November 1955, later the same year the joke had already appeared in print with an unnamed professor and an unnamed maestro (Popik ↗). Heifetz’s own Wikiquote page ↗ does not carry it either.
Wikipedia’s account states that attributions to Jack Benny are mistaken ↗, and that it is uncertain whether he ever used the joke at all.

Carnegie Hall’s own archivist, Gino Francesconi, favours a version told by the wife of violinist Mischa Elman, in which Elman makes the quip when approached by tourists as he leaves the hall’s backstage entrance after an unsatisfactory rehearsal (Wikipedia ↗). It is a family recollection, not a contemporary record, and it does not displace the 1955 printings.

The triple is not in the earliest tellings. Quote Investigator ↗ notes that the March 1955 version does not repeat the word — the maestro simply says “Practice!” The tripled form turns up by 1959 in a Yankee Stadium spin-off QI quotes from Baseball Digest, and a doubled “Practice, practice” appears in a New York Times aside of 26 March 1961 (Popik ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: No early version of the joke names any musician at all: the two earliest tellings, in separate newspaper humor columns in 1955, hand the line to an anonymous “absent-minded music professor” and an anonymous “absent-minded maestro.” The famous names — Heifetz, Rubinstein, Gillespie, Benny — were all fitted to it afterwards (Popik ↗; Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke with no father
lead: Carnegie Hall opened in 1891, and for most of the century that followed nobody seems to have made this joke — or at least nobody wrote it down. It surfaces, apparently fully formed, in two American newspaper humor columns in the opening months of 1955, and in both the man giving directions is a nobody: an “absent-minded music professor” in one, an “absent-minded maestro” in the other. Vaudeville is the usual guess for where it came from before that, but a guess is all it is.

What happened next is the ordinary life cycle of a good joke: it acquired a famous mouth. Bennett Cerf hung it on Jascha Heifetz later in 1955 — carefully, as “rumor” — and from there the punchline passed around to a beatnik, a bopper, a cab driver, Dizzy Gillespie, Jack Benny and, most durably, Arthur Rubinstein. None of the named musicians has a contemporary source behind it. Carnegie Hall’s own archivist favours a different candidate still, the violinist Mischa Elman, on the strength of a story told by Elman’s wife — which is a guess too, and honestly labelled as one.
context.detailsSummary: The variants, and where the third “practice” came from
detailsBody: The tripled punchline everyone quotes is itself a later addition. Quote Investigator notes that the March 1955 column does not repeat the word at all — the maestro just says “Practice!” The full triple shows up by 1959, and not about Carnegie Hall: Quote Investigator quotes a Baseball Digest item in which the comedian Al Schacht, asked outside his New York restaurant how to get to Yankee Stadium, replies “Practice, practice, practice!” A doubled “Practice, practice” appears in a New York Times aside of 26 March 1961, which already dismisses the whole thing as an “ancient wheeze.”

The joke bred variants faster than it bred evidence. Popik’s chronology includes a beatnik telling in the Lima (Ohio) News of 9 December 1960 — “Practice, man, practice” — and a 1957 Washington Post item crediting the Journal of the American Medical Association with the Heifetz version. Popik’s entry also points to a Carnegie Deli spin-off with its own separate page. That is the signature of folklore rather than authorship: the frame changes freely, the punchline does not, and no telling earlier than 1955 has yet been found.
context.pull: In the first telling, the maestro has no name. He never really acquired one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator names E. E. Kenyon's syndicated column "The Wit Parade" of 13 March 1955 as the joke's earliest known appearance, transcribes it verbatim (an unnamed "absent-minded maestro" racing up Seventh Avenue who answers "Practice!"), notes that in this version the word practice is not repeated, credits Barry Popik's Big Apple page as its source, and quotes a 1959 Baseball Digest variant in which Al Schacht answers "Practice, practice, practice!" about Yankee Stadium. QI asserts no originator.

Barry Popik's Big Apple entry transcribes seven dated citations: 1 January 1955 Philadelphia Tribune ("absent-minded music professor" / "Practice constantly"); 13 March 1955 Washington Post "The Wit Parade" ("absent-minded maestro" / "Practice!"); 9 November 1955 Titusville Herald, Bennett Cerf's "Try and Stop Me" ("Rumor is that a pedestrian in Manhattan stopped Jascha Heifetz..."); Cerf's The Life of the Party (Doubleday, 1956), p. 335; 26 April 1957 Washington Post citing JAMA; 9 December 1960 Lima (OH) News (beatnik, "Practice, man, practice"); 26 March 1961 New York Times (cab driver, "Practice, practice", called an "ancient wheeze"). It also notes the Carnegie Deli spin-off joke.

Wikipedia's Carnegie Hall article, section "Famous joke", states the joke's origins remain a mystery and its earliest known print appearances date from 1955; that attributions to Jack Benny are mistaken and it is uncertain if he ever used the joke; that alternatives to Heifetz include an unnamed beatnik, bopper or "absent-minded maestro", plus Arthur Rubinstein and Dizzy Gillespie; and that Carnegie Hall archivist Gino Francesconi favours a version told by the wife of violinist Mischa Elman, set at the hall's backstage entrance after an unsatisfactory rehearsal. It quotes the Cerf 1956 text and cites the book at page 335.

Wikiquote's Arthur Rubinstein page does not contain the "How do you get to Carnegie Hall? Practice" quote in any section; its headings are Quotes, Attributed, About and External links (there is no Sourced or Misattributed section). The page gives Rubinstein's dates as 28 January 1887 – 20 December 1982 and describes him as a Polish-American pianist.

Wikiquote's Jascha Heifetz page does not contain the Carnegie Hall practice quote in any section, and gives his dates as 2 February 1901 – 10 December 1987, describing him as a Lithuanian-born American violinist.

Steinway & Sons' feature states: "The punch line is often attributed to Jascha Heifetz or Artur Rubinstein, sometimes to an anonymous musician or taxi driver, and once even to a beatnik, who, in a 1960 telling, replied 'Practice, man, practice.'"
